title: Building trust and confidence a must before going to India with a wish list, experts advise Nepali leadership - The Kathmandu Post
description: Building trust and confidence a must before going to India with a wish list, experts advise Nepali leadership  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
As preparations ramp up for Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s India visit, observers have cautioned Kathmandu against approaching New Delhi with an extensive wish list, arguing that Nepal should instead focus on restoring the political trust and confidence with its southern neighbour.

“Ask no favour and take no wish list along. Talk to the other side eye to eye as an equal counterpart,” former foreign secretary Madhu Raman Acharya advises the Nepali prime minister. “Concentrate on issues that need to be resolved at the highest political level. Focus on building trust and confidence. Let the mechanisms work on the issues; the rest will follow.”

India’s Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri returned to Delhi on Thursday after two days of engagements in Kathmandu. In a trip focussed on Prime Minister Shah’s visit to Kathmandu, Misri discussed a range of proposals and agendas put forward by the Nepali side.

Misri paid courtesy calls on the prime minister, Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal, Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha and Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal. In these meetings and others with senior officials, potential agendas for the prime minister’s visit were discussed. Both sides have tentatively agreed November 22-25 for Prime Minister Shah's first official bilateral visit since taking office in March.

Misri focussed largely on government-to-government engagement as the visiting secretary held fewer political meetings in Kathmandu. The reading of the Indian establishment is that there is less fragmentation in Nepali politics this time. According to a Nepal observer in New Delhi, this is the reason why Misri did not have many political meetings and parleys in Kathmandu, in a break from past visits from India that saw meetings with Nepali leaders across the political spectrum.

The two neighbours need to restore confidence in order to normalise their relations, Acharya stressed. “There must be a solid understanding between the top leadership [on both sides].”

Once confidence and trust are restored, things will move faster, Acharya said about Nepal-India cooperation.

Besides infrastructure projects, Nepal is seeking an early review of the Nepal-India Trade Treaty, which is currently scheduled for renewal in 2030. The proposed revision aims to address non-tariff barriers and difficulties faced by Nepali exporters.

Nepal has also requested access to two additional Indian ports in Gujarat and Odisha to facilitate trade with third countries.

Although preliminary discussions have taken place on several proposals, no agreements have yet been finalised. India's response will be particularly important on the proposed financial assistance package, rupee-denominated loans, additional air-entry routes, railway expansion and revision of the trade treaty, government officials said.

“If we do not have good relations at the top level, nothing will happen at the bottom. So building confidence is very important. The prime minister should focus on building trust and confidence with the Indian leadership,” former secretary Acharya told the Post.

In New Delhi, the mood is positive, said Ranjit Rae, former Indian ambassador to Nepal. He said a series of back-to-back visits by officials and political leaders from both countries had helped prepare the ground for the current engagement.

“Misri’s visit has added positive vibes to the relationship. The overall attitude in New Delhi is positive and problem-solving. There is a growing sense that we should take a pragmatic approach towards resolving differences,” Rae told the Post from New Delhi.

Several ministers of the Rastriya Swatantra Party government have visited India in recent months. They include Finance Minister Wagle, Foreign Minister Khanal and Home Minister Sudan Gurung.

Before returning to Delhi, Misri met only two political leaders—RSP President Rabi Lamichhane and Nepali Congress President Gagan Thapa.

During previous high-level visits, Indian leaders and officials would typically meet representatives of the Madhesh-based parties and other political forces. But Misri did not meet any Madheshi leader in Kathmandu this time.

“But they are in communication with us,” said Surendra Kumar Jha, a Madheshi leader close to Mahantha Thakur. “We heard that meetings with Madheshi leaders were not on the itinerary,” he said.

Nepal–India relations must be guided by the well-being and prosperity of the people of both countries, said former Nepali Army general Binoj Basnyat. The objective, he said, should be to advance economic statecraft through development-oriented diplomacy, transforming geographical proximity and historical ties into tangible opportunities for shared growth.

“Today’s national mandate is not about ideological alignment or political competence defined by ideology. It’s about delivering reforms, strengthening institutional capacity and pursuing an opportunity-driven foreign policy,” Basnyat said.

“Diplomacy must increasingly serve economic interests—mobilising investment, expanding trade, strengthening connectivity, creating employment and unlocking shared development opportunities.”

The priority is to move from political rhetoric to tangible results, from traditional diplomacy to development diplomacy, and from managing differences to building mutual prosperity, Basnyat suggested.

In Kathmandu, Misri and Nepali officials discussed Nepal’s proposal for a $2 billion economic assistance package from India, alongside major infrastructure, trade, energy and connectivity initiatives.

Nepal has sought $1 billion in grants and another $1 billion in concessional loans to finance various development projects.

Of the proposed grant assistance, $500 million would be allocated for the construction of the Butwal–Pokhara Expressway, while the remaining $500 million would support the reconstruction of infrastructure damaged by the Bhotekoshi flash flood. The concessional loans would primarily finance hydropower projects and electricity transmission lines.

Nepal has also proposed receiving loans in Indian rupees instead of US dollars to minimise foreign exchange risks and make future debt repayments more predictable.

In the water resources sector, the two sides have agreed to convene a meeting on the Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project to address outstanding water-sharing issues. Other proposals include constructing an LPG pipeline from Motihari in India to Sarlahi, extending the existing Raxaul-Amalekhgunj petroleum pipeline to Bhandara in Chitwan, and building another petroleum pipeline from Siliguri towards Jhapa.

Beyond infrastructure, Kathmandu has proposed establishing branches of India's prestigious Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) and Indian Institutes of Management (IIMs) in Nepal. It has also sought cooperation in areas such as artificial intelligence and technical assistance for cricket development through training, capacity building and knowledge exchange.

Meanwhile, preparations are under way for the joint inauguration of several Indian-assisted projects, including the Bhairahawa Integrated Check Post, the Police Training Centre in Panauti and a bridge in Darchula.

The Butwal-Pokhara Expressway is among Nepal’s major infrastructure priorities. Estimated to cost around $750 million, the project aims to reduce travel time between the Indian border and Pokhara to about two hours while promoting tourism, trade and transportation. The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank has already conducted a feasibility study for the project.

During Misri’s visit, a trial run was also conducted on the Janakpur-Ayodhya rail route to promote religious tourism.

“The trial run of the Ayodhya-Janakpur rail service is a good step forward,” outgoing Indian Ambassador to Nepal Naveen Srivastava wrote on social media platform X. He said the commencement of regular train services between the two historic cities would reinforce the strong cultural and traditional bonds between India and Nepal and boost bilateral tourism.

Nepal has also proposed extending railway lines from Janakpur through Bardibas to Nijgadh, as well as connecting Raxaul in India with Birgunj and Pathlaiya.

title: Deepfake Trust Deficit - The Rising Nepal
description: Deepfake Trust Deficit  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
KAMUD GAUTAM

For years, people have been told not to believe everything they read on the internet. Today, the warning has become much more serious: we may not be able to believe everything we see or hear either. Deepfake technology is spreading fast, and it presents a new crisis of trust on the internet that societies like Nepal cannot afford to overlook.

Deepfakes are artificial intelligence-made digitally manipulated images, videos, or audio recordings. They can make it look like someone is saying or doing something that never happened. Initially, this type of technology was popularised through entertainment and social media trends. But its increasing sophistication has made it a powerful tool for fraud, misinformation, harassment and political manipulation.

The risk is in how persuasive these materials can be. Within minutes, a fake video of a public figure can be shared on Facebook, TikTok, YouTube or messaging apps. Before fact-checkers have a chance to respond, thousands of people may have already watched, shared and believed it. It is especially worrying in a country where social media is turning into an important source of news.

Nepal has already witnessed how quickly rumours, edited clips and misleading posts can influence public opinion. That problem could be made much worse by deepfakes. A fake speech by a politician, a bogus announcement by a government official, or a doctored video of a celebrity might cause confusion, anger or panic. The consequences could be even more serious if there are elections, natural disasters or times of national tension.

It's not just politics at stake. Criminals can use AI to create voices that sound like family members, bosses, or bank officials. A person might receive a phone call that sounds exactly like a relative who needs money urgently. Businesses could be attacked with fake video calls or forged audio instructions. Online blackmail and character assassination also threaten women and young people.

The problem is so serious because deepfakes don’t only create false information; they also undermine confidence in real evidence. When people learn that videos and voices can be made up, they can also dismiss actual recordings as “fake.” This produces what experts often call a crisis of authenticity. In such a context, truth is harder to prove and public trust in journalism, institutions and even personal communication begins to erode.

The answer cannot be to distrust everything on the Internet. Instead, Nepal needs better online literacy, better fact-checking, responsible journalism and updated laws. Schools and universities must teach students to check sources, identify doctored material, and stop and think before sharing sensational content. Media houses should have clear ways to verify suspicious video and audio. Technology companies also need to improve tools for detecting and labelling synthetic content.

Government agencies are as important. Freedom of expression should be preserved, but existing cyber laws need to be reviewed to include harmful use of AI-generated media. Law enforcement agencies require technical capacity to investigate digital impersonation and fraud. Political parties and public institutions should also pledge to not deploy misleading synthetic media.

For regular internet users, a few habits can help: verify the source, cross-reference the information with reputable news outlets, be alert to strange facial movements or inconsistent audio, and do not forward unconfirmed content just because it’s shocking.

Deepfakes are not only a technological problem. They’re a matter of trust. The promise of the internet was to provide faster access to information. Its next test is to ensure people can distinguish information from fabrication. In the modern era of artificial intelligence, protecting truth may become one of the most important duties of citizens and institutions alike.

title: Economic Digest: A Snapshot of Nepal’s Business News - Khabarhub
description: Economic Digest: A Snapshot of Nepal’s Business News  Khabarhub
publisher.title: Khabarhub
full_article:
KATHMANDU: Economic Digest presents a brief yet comprehensive roundup of major business developments in Nepal, delivered in clear and accessible summaries.

Recent developments across Nepal highlight a growing emphasis on institutional accountability, economic empowerment, disaster recovery and improved public service delivery. The blacklisting of 20 contractors and suppliers by the Public Procurement Monitoring Office signals efforts to enforce contractual discipline and strengthen transparency in government-funded projects. Similarly, the planned deployment of civil servants to provincial and local governments reflects the need to address administrative gaps and improve service delivery under the federal system.

Economic initiatives are also gaining attention, particularly Koshi Province’s allocation of Rs. 8 billion in concessional loans to promote youth entrepreneurship, boost domestic production and generate employment. The planned Suryodaya Tea Festival in Ilam further reflects efforts to connect local industries with tourism, market expansion and regional economic opportunities.

Meanwhile, preparations by the Nepal Electricity Authority to meet peak demand of 1,700 MW during Laxmi Puja demonstrate the importance of infrastructure readiness and reliable essential services during major festivals. However, the temporary suspension of waste management in Kathmandu Valley exposes operational vulnerabilities in urban service delivery.

Private-sector participation in disaster recovery, illustrated by Thamel Tourism Development Council’s Rs. 1.64 million contribution to flood rehabilitation, underscores the importance of collective responsibility. Nepal Telecom’s doorstep SIM delivery initiative also demonstrates how institutional collaboration and digital services can improve public convenience.

Overall, these developments point to the need for stronger governance, effective coordination, infrastructure resilience and inclusive economic growth to translate policy initiatives into tangible public benefits.

Public Procurement Monitoring Office blacklists 20 contractors and suppliers

The Public Procurement Monitoring Office (PPMO) has blacklisted 20 construction contractors and supplier companies for failing to meet their contractual obligations. According to a public notice issued on Saturday, the action was taken under Section 63(1) of the Public Procurement Act, 2007, following recommendations from various public agencies. The blacklisted companies will be barred from participating in public procurement processes and government bidding for periods ranging from one year and six months to two years. The action is aimed at enforcing contractual compliance and strengthening transparency and accountability in public procurement and government-funded projects.

NEA forecasts peak electricity demand of 1,700 MW on Laxmi Puja

The Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) has projected peak electricity demand to reach around 1,700 megawatts on the evening of Laxmi Puja during this year’s Tihar festival. The authority said domestic electricity generation is expected to reach approximately 2,500 megawatts during the period, which would be sufficient to meet national demand and ensure a smooth power supply. The NEA has made special arrangements to maintain a reliable, uninterrupted and quality electricity supply throughout the Tihar and Chhath festivals. Technical teams, emergency repair units and regional distribution offices have been instructed to remain prepared to respond promptly to any potential disruptions in the electricity supply. The authority has also directed officials concerned to ensure that telephone calls received through the no-light service are answered regularly and that consumer complaints regarding power outages are addressed without delay.

Koshi Province allocates Rs. 8 billion for youth entrepreneurship and concessional loans

The Koshi Province Government has allocated Rs. 8 billion in its current fiscal year’s budget to provide concessional loans to young entrepreneurs seeking to establish and operate small and medium-sized enterprises. The programme, announced during a press conference in Khandbari, Sankhuwasabha, on Saturday, aims to promote youth entrepreneurship, increase domestic production and generate employment opportunities within the province. Under the initiative, eligible young entrepreneurs will be able to access concessional loans for a period of three years. The provincial government said it had prioritised youth-focused economic initiatives and policy reforms to strengthen the provincial economy and create employment opportunities despite limited financial resources and constraints on development expenditure. The government has also emphasised infrastructure development, economic growth and good governance as key priorities for the province.

Kathmandu Valley waste management to be suspended for two days during Tihar

Waste management services across the Kathmandu Valley will remain disrupted on November 10 and 11 as employees at the Bancharedanda landfill site observe holidays during the Tihar festival. The Kathmandu Metropolitan City’s Environment Management Department has urged residents to refrain from dumping household waste indiscriminately on roadsides and in public places during the temporary closure of the landfill site. The department said regular waste collection and disposal services would resume from November 12. Residents have been requested to manage and store household waste responsibly until regular services resume.

Ministry to deploy civil servants to provincial and local governments to address staff shortages

The Ministry of Land Management, Cooperatives, Federal Affairs and General Administration has decided to deploy non-gazetted first-class civil servants to provincial and local government offices to address staffing shortages. The decision, taken on Saturday under Section 9(1) of the Employee Adjustment Act, 2019, aims to facilitate the delivery of public services in offices facing vacancies in approved positions. Provincial and local governments have been asked to submit details of their staffing requirements to facilitate the deployment process. Officials assigned to the respective offices will receive their salaries and allowances directly from the provincial or local governments where they are posted.

Ilam to host tea festival to promote tourism and expand market opportunities

The first Suryodaya Tea Festival 2026 is scheduled to take place in Kanyam, Ilam, on November 21 and 22, with the objective of promoting tea tourism and expanding market opportunities for locally produced tea. The festival will also highlight the development of a 25.5-kilometre tea trail connecting Kanyam and Shree Antu, an initiative aimed at promoting tourism through the region’s tea-growing landscape. Organised jointly by Suryodaya Municipality, the Koshi Province Government and tourism stakeholders associated with the trail, the event is estimated to cost Rs. 1.5 million. The two-day festival will feature tea trail races covering 12.5 kilometres for men and nine kilometres for women, alongside tea-tasting exhibitions, discussions on climate adaptation and cultural programmes. Organisers expect the festival to attract more than 10,000 domestic and international visitors, providing an opportunity to showcase Ilam’s tea industry, tourism potential and cultural heritage.

Thamel Tourism Development Council contributes Rs. 1.64 million to PM’s Relief Fund

The Thamel Tourism Development Council has contributed Rs. 1.64 million to the Prime Minister’s Relief Fund to support the reconstruction and rehabilitation of areas affected by the Bhotekoshi floods in Rasuwa on August 26. The Council handed over the amount through Kathmandu Chief District Officer Ishwori Raj Poudel last evening. At a programme titled ‘Discussion and Interaction on Peace and Security in Thamel Area’, organised by the Council in Thamel on Friday evening, Council Chairman Rajuman Dangol handed over the cheque to Chief District Officer Poudel. On the occasion, Poudel highly appreciated the support extended by homeowners and businesspeople in the Thamel area to disaster victims. Council Treasurer Kinchu Lhamu Bhutia Shrestha said the contribution was made with the objective of supporting the reconstruction of disaster-affected areas, restoring damaged physical infrastructure and providing relief to affected communities.

Nepal Telecom to deliver SIM cards to customers’ doorsteps through postal service

Nepal Telecom has introduced a doorstep SIM card delivery service in Parsa district in collaboration with the Department of Postal Services, aiming to make its services more accessible and convenient for customers. Under an agreement between Nepal Telecom and the postal department, customers in Parsa can now receive Nepal Telecom SIM cards at their home addresses through the postal service. According to Namanath Yadav, postal officer at the District Post Office, the service has been launched to save customers the time and effort required to visit telecom offices to obtain SIM cards. Customers can apply for a SIM card by completing Nepal Telecom’s online application form and receive it at their registered addresses through postal employees.

title: It's a dog's life - Nepali Times
description: It's a dog's life  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
As the city lights up in celebration of Tihar, the most anticipated day for Nepal’s dogs and their parents arrives: कुकुर पुजा.

Yet, it is a mixed blessing for our furry friends. Nepalis worship them as the guardians of the gates of heaven, garland them with marigold and offer them treats in the morning, and in the evening spook the doggies with firecrackers.

This Kukur Tihar may also be a time to give a thought to the many pets that have been separated from their families during the recent floods on the Trisuli and Budi Gandaki. Two dogs in particular have captured the hearts of people worldwide.

Seti (pictured, left) belongs to Dayaram Karki from Dharche, and was taken away in the Budi Gandaki flood on 11 October. She was swept down to Jagat and marooned on a sandbar, surviving for two weeks on biscuits thrown across the raging water.

Seti was finally rescued after a three-day effort led by Animal Nepal which deployed professional white water canoe guides to bring her home. A video of the daring rescue across the turbulent river has been viewed around the world.

Then there is the story of a black-and-white dog in Trisuli which just would not abandon the spot where its family’s house used to be in the 26 August flood. The dog has a collar, but no one seems to know its name since the entire neighbourhood is gone.

The dog sits quietly at what was once its family’s courtyard, sometimes digging in the sand. His unwavering loyalty has become a heartbreaking symbol of the attachment of a human’s best friend.

Social media has played a vital role in recent years in disseminating information about missing dogs, or getting people interested in adopting abandoned ones from shelters. And that same digital space has also highlighted human-dog bonds during darker times.

SOCIAL ANIMALS

Rajiv Lama is better known by his social media handle, karzen_kanchi because he posts videos of his five adorable canines as they go about their daily activities around his home, showing amazing obedience and affection. Videos of the dogs posted on social media are viewed by millions around the world.

Kanchi is a nine-year-old Labrador mix, and Kali a two-year-old Golden Retriever and German Shepherd mix. Lama also has two street rescues, Gori and Khaire. And Gori now has a daughter, Pari.

title: Nepal Must Follow Balanced Diplomacy - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal Must Follow Balanced Diplomacy  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s anticipated visit to India is expected in the second half of November 2026. Indian Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri visited Kathmandu and returned to New Delhi with the dates of the visit under the confirmation process, in view of the Tihar festival. It is an important opportunity to promote Nepal’s national interests through constructive engagement with India. Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has stated on record that both governments want the visit to be fruitful and result-oriented.

The distinction between substantive and peripheral noise matters, particularly as Nepal seeks economic recovery, stronger and sustained connectivity, access to greater energy exports, and effective reconstruction after devastating floods. A high-level visit is neither an achievement in itself nor a concession to the host country. Its meaningfulness depends on what Nepal negotiates, what the two sides agree upon and, above all, what they subsequently implement.

India's invitation

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi extended an invitation to Shah soon after the formation of his government in March 2026. India publicly confirmed the invitation in July. In August, Shah met the Indian Ambassador, Naveen Srivastava, at the Prime Minister’s Office. The official account of the meeting broadly emphasised the strengthening of Nepal-India relations, development partnership and cooperation in areas of mutual interest. On the same day, Shah also met Chinese Ambassador Zhang Maoming, who conveyed an invitation to visit China. The sequence of the two meetings indicates that both immediate neighbours are keen to promote relations with Nepal.

These engagements offer an important historical and diplomatic reference. Nepal has longstanding relations with both neighbours, and the Prime Minister’s engagement with each should be guided by Nepal’s interests, established diplomatic principles and mutual respect. The Kathmandu Post (August 1, 2026) commented that neither a visit to India nor a subsequent visit to China should automatically be interpreted as a strategic alignment against the other. Shah initially did not undertake any foreign visits during his first year in office. His eventual participation in the United Nations General Assembly in September demonstrated that circumstances and national priorities can warrant reconsideration. The proposed India visit should similarly be understood as an instrument of statecraft rather than a test of sheer political ongoing.

Finance Minister Dr Swarnim Wagle’s September visit to New Delhi provides a more political than economic angle. Bilateral economic partnership is a priority in this era. Efficient, unhindered and sustained multi-level international connectivity tops the priority. China, for example, in the context of the bilateral review of the feasibility study of the Kerung-Kathmandu Railway, candidly questioned Nepal on how it will be connected with other railway lines to optimize the benefits. Nepal indeed needs progress on unresolved questions concerning Lipulek, Kalapani and Limpiyadhura, air routes, border and national trade imbalances and water-resource cooperation. Diplomatic maturity means pursuing cooperation where neighbourly interests converge while maintaining a clear, principled position where differences remain.

The June visit to India by Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) President Rabi Lamichhane attracted considerable attention in Nepal and India. His meetings with Indian leaders, including Prime Minister Modi, generated speculation about political signalling and the relative roles of the party chairman and Nepal’s Prime Minister. Some Indian commentary interpreted the reception as a message to Kathmandu. Such interpretations are legitimate subjects of media analysis, but they do not, by themselves, establish the intentions of either government.

Lamichhane’s separate visit to India in October, which he described as personal and religious, should not be taken at par with his earlier political engagement. It is unworthy to reduce the Prime Minister’s forthcoming state-level diplomacy to a presumed contest between two leaders of the same governing party. The constitutional responsibility for conducting Nepal’s government-to-government relations rests with the state institutions mandated to do so.

Domestic concerns nevertheless deserve attention. Opposition parties have previously challenged Shah’s remarks concerning the sensitive border question, arguing that his words could weaken Nepal’s position. RSP leaders, meanwhile, have reaffirmed their commitment to sovereignty and the peaceful diplomatic resolution of disputes. These competing positions underline the need for clarity, consultation and national consensus on territorial integrity issues. They should not become an excuse either to obstruct constructive state diplomacy or to silence legitimate domestic scrutiny.

Media commentary in India has examined whether Nepal’s new leadership is recalibrating its relationship with New Delhi. Chinese official communications, meanwhile, have emphasised traditional friendship and mutually beneficial cooperation with Nepal. Broader regional analysis has also highlighted Nepal’s efforts to attract investment and technology from both neighbours. Such perspectives deserve consideration. Nepal must evaluate external expectations against its own development priorities and sovereign judgement.

National interests

Prime Minister Shah’s upcoming visit should therefore be neither romanticised as a diplomatic breakthrough in advance nor dismissed through suspicion and partisan criticism. Its success will depend on concrete, measurable outcomes, credible implementation schedules and continued dialogue on difficult questions. Nepal should approach India with friendship, confidence and clarity. Equally, balanced relations with China should remain a normal and independent element of Nepal’s foreign policy. Thus, relations should be nurtured multilaterally with neighbours from a balance per se in the dynamics across the Trans-Himalaya. The substance is straightforward: Promotion of multiple international connectivity and progress on outstanding disputes. The peripheral noise concerns pressures, personalities, protocol, presumed geopolitical messages and premature claims of victory or surrender.

For Nepal, the ultimate measure of this visit will not be who receives the greatest ceremonial attention, which leader attracts the loudest headlines, or which neighbouring capital claims diplomatic advantage. It will be whether the engagement strengthens Nepal’s indigenous capacity to pursue development, safeguard sovereignty and maintain mutually beneficial relations with its neighbours. That is the difference between diplomatic theatre and effective statecraft—and the standard the conscious Nepali public reasonably expects.





(Dr. Gautam is the secretary general of China Study Centre Nepal).

title: Nepal reports sugar stocks for Tihar, LPG shortage persists — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal reports sugar stocks for Tihar, LPG shortage persists — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, government agencies and traders have reported sufficient stocks of sugar, rice, pulses and vegetable oil ahead of the Tihar festival. At the same time, a shortage of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) continues in the country, Kathmandu Post reports.

Sugar stocks and subsidised sales

According to the Salt Trading Corporation, Nepal's monthly demand for sugar is 20,000–25,000 tonnes, rising to around 30,000 tonnes during the Dashain, Tihar and Chhath festivals. Annual demand is estimated at 300,000 tonnes: about 200,000 tonnes are supplied by domestic production, while the remainder is imported.

The Salt Trading Corporation has around 11,700 tonnes of sugar and has purchased another 12,000 tonnes from local producers. The government set the corporation a deadline of October 20 to import 25,000 tonnes of sugar for the festive season, but it imported around 16,000 tonnes. Corporation representative Kumar Rajbanshi said stocks were sufficient for Tihar and that the deadline for further imports should be extended.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Before the holidays, authorities opened 38 subsidised sales outlets across the country, where sugar is sold for 100 Nepalese rupees per kilogram. The state-owned Food Management and Trading Company Limited has around 1,250 tonnes of sugar in stock and sells it for 109 rupees per kilogram in Kathmandu and through outlets in other parts of the country. According to trade representatives, the regular price is around 110 rupees, although sugar imported outside state structures is sold for 120–135 rupees per kilogram.

LPG problems persist

The LPG shortage, which began in February, continues to affect consumers. Nepal LP Gas Industry Association President Diwan Chand linked the situation to reduced imports and warned that demand for gas would rise as temperatures fall because of more active use of heaters and water heaters.

Nepal Oil Corporation says import volumes for Tihar are sufficient, and shortages in certain areas result from delays in delivering cylinders to dealers. According to corporation representative Manoj Thakur, 149 and 137 gas tankers were loaded over the past two days, respectively.

title: Opinion | The families who wait - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | The families who wait  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
In almost every village in Nepal, someone is missing from almost every household. A husband in Qatar. A son in Malaysia. A daughter in the Gulf or a brother in Japan. People who may not come home for years pay for the new roof, the school fees and the motorbike in the yard.

The economic story is well known. According to Nepal Rastra Bank, remittance inflows in fiscal year 2025/26 reached Rs2.363 trillion, equal to about 35.8 percent of GDP. The Department of Foreign Employment issued 792,187 labour approvals in the same year, down from 839,266 in 2024/25 but still enormous for a country of Nepal’s size.

The human story is told less often, especially the part about those who stay behind.

A burden carried at home

When a man migrates for work, his wife often takes on the jobs of two people. She manages the farm, the household, the children and his ageing parents, while living in her in-laws’ home. She handles money that arrives irregularly and debts taken on to pay recruitment fees. She is watched closely by relatives and neighbours, and judged for how she spends or behaves.

The evidence suggests that this weighs heavily. A study published in BMJ Open on December 15, 2025, surveyed 179 wives of migrant workers in Jhapa. It found that 54.7 percent showed symptoms of depression, 53.1 percent symptoms of anxiety and 60.9 percent symptoms of stress.

These are not small numbers. They suggest that, in some communities, distress is the ordinary condition of the women holding families together.

There is also fear. The Foreign Employment Board recorded 1,438 deaths of Nepali migrant workers abroad between July 17, 2025, and June 14, 2026, more than four every day. In the fiscal year before that, it recorded 1,583.

Behind each of those deaths is a family that received a phone call it had dreaded. And behind them are many more families who live with the same possibility. A missed call, a phone that goes unanswered for a day or a rumour about an accident at a construction site can bring days of anxiety.

Children are affected too. They may miss a parent deeply, struggle at school or feel they must grow up quickly. Grandparents who care for them may be unwell themselves.

The government and development partners already run programmes for migrant workers, from pre-departure orientation to welfare funds. Those programmes could do more for families at home.

First, local health posts and female community health volunteers are trusted in their communities. With basic training, they could recognise signs of depression and anxiety among migrants’ families and refer those who need more help.

Second, ward offices and local governments could support women’s groups where wives of migrant workers can meet, share advice and simply be with others who understand. Isolation is one of the heaviest parts of waiting.

Third, pre-departure orientation could include a session for families, not only workers, covering how to stay connected, how to manage money together and where to find support.

Fourth, when a worker dies abroad, families need practical and emotional support quickly, not only compensation that may take months to arrive.

Staying in touch also matters for mental health. Many families now talk daily by video call, which can be a lifeline. But calls are often rushed, interrupted by bad connections or work shifts, and full of practical matters. There is little space for feelings.

Writing can help fill that gap. A 2006 meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin found that writing about difficult experiences brings small but real benefits for well-being. In my work on blog psychology , I have seen how writing helps people name feelings they might otherwise swallow. A wife who keeps a short journal, or a worker who writes letters home about how he is really doing, may find it easier to share what a hurried phone call cannot hold. Children can write or draw for an absent parent, and keep a record of the months apart.

Some families may want to share these experiences more widely, and their stories can help others feel less alone. Others will prefer privacy, and that is equally valid.

Foreign employment has lifted many Nepali families out of poverty, and it will remain part of the country’s life for years to come. But its true cost includes the anxiety, loneliness and grief of the people at home. Recognising that cost, and supporting the families who carry it, is a matter of fairness as well as health.

title: Opinion | Nepal’s 250-year-old foreign policy still works. Why does no one use it? - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | Nepal’s 250-year-old foreign policy still works. Why does no one use it?  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal’s most durable foreign policy fits inside a single image: a yam between two rocks . A king coined it more than 250 years ago, and the country has been quoting it, and misreading it, ever since. Its sharpest lesson has little to do with geography. It concerns discipline, which is precisely what Nepali diplomacy has lacked.

That lack is now the Balendra Shah government’s to fix. Elected in March on a strong public mandate for change, the prime minister inherited three decades of improvised diplomacy, and his government’s early hesitation to engage envoys directly , along with a taste for informal channels, risked repeating it. Advisers reportedly held key meetings without the Foreign Ministry’s formal involvement. Direct engagement with India, China and other partners has since resumed, but two repairs remain: make the ministry the only channel for diplomacy, and replace reactive balancing with a strategy Nepal chooses for itself .

The doctrine began with Prithvi Narayan Shah. In his Dibya Upadesh , the king who unified Nepal sized up a small state squeezed between the expanding British East India Company to the south and the Qing Empire to the north. His answer was practical: befriend both, bow to neither, guard sovereignty and territorial integrity, and avoid needless confrontation. It was a theory of survival, defensive and cautious, resting on self-reliance and limited contact with the outside world.

The Ranas broke with it. After Jung Bahadur Rana seized power in 1846, foreign policy bent toward British imperial interests, and its chief purpose became preserving an autocracy, often at the nation’s expense. Kathmandu gave the British generous military help while keeping thin ties with China and Tibet. As the empire withdrew from South Asia after the Second World War, the Ranas sought recognition elsewhere, establishing relations with the United States in 1947 and France in 1949 and applying for United Nations membership. The goal was legitimacy for the regime, not for the nation.

King Mahendra revived the idea and made it assertive. Where Prithvi Narayan Shah practised caution, Mahendra practised active neutrality, using treaties, aid, bilateral diplomacy and global forums to widen Nepal’s room for manoeuvre. He formally associated Nepal with the Non-Aligned Movement and adapted the old principles to the Cold War: non-alignment, peaceful coexistence, non-interference. His refusal to give India direct military support in the 1962 Sino-Indian war showed the doctrine at work. The aim was no longer survival alone. It was development assistance, recognition and autonomy.

King Birendra tried to write neutrality into international commitments. His Zone of Peace proposal , first presented at the Non-Aligned Movement summit in 1973, sought a pledge that Nepali territory would never be used for hostile activities against any other country. More than 110 countries endorsed it. India, which saw a challenge to its own security framework, did not, and the idea stalled. Birendra kept China as a diplomatic counterweight, kept ties with the Cold War powers, helped found SAARC in 1985, and steered by Panchsheel, the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence.

Since multiparty democracy returned in 1990, continuity has broken. Political instability and frequent changes of government left little room for long-term planning. Successive governments swung between closer engagement with India and a lean toward China, depending on their need to survive or their ideological leanings. Foreign policy began to reflect the preferences of individuals rather than the priorities of a nation, and delicate matters moved through informal channels. Institutions, transparency and public confidence paid for it.

The 2015 unofficial Indian blockade showed the cost. Kathmandu turned to China for alternative supplies , a sensible reflex, but with no long-term strategy behind it, the tilt could not alter Nepal’s structural and geographic ties with India. A country that lurches from one neighbour to the other, depending on who holds office, soon earns a reputation. Nepal’s is closer to that of a ship without a rudder than to that of a reliable, predictable partner.

The first repair is institutional. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs must be restored as the sole channel for diplomacy. Informal envoys and parallel channels that bypass protocol confuse foreign partners and weaken the institutions meant to protect the national interest. Political leaders should set direction; professionals should conduct the talks, in coordination and on the record. The ministry has begun drafting country-specific strategy papers , and that discipline should extend to every channel.

The second repair is strategic. Nepal must stop balancing in reaction to events and build a proactive policy around economic diplomacy, regional connectivity and multilateral engagement. Mahendra’s example is the guide: keep the core of the Yam Doctrine and adapt it to the world as it is. In that world, a landlocked country can become a transit and connectivity hub between its two large economic neighbours.

None of it works without predictable, transparent and regular dialogue with both neighbours. Relations with New Delhi and Beijing are not a zero-sum game; each deserves cultivation on its own merits and mutual interests. Nepal should also make far greater use of BIMSTEC , BBIN and the United Nations. And a foreign policy white paper, led by the Foreign Ministry and approved by Parliament, would carry policy across changes of government .

title: From flood-hit areas to crime scenes, Nepal’s police dogs sniff out vital clues - The Kathmandu Post
description: From flood-hit areas to crime scenes, Nepal’s police dogs sniff out vital clues  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The Bhotekoshi floods on August 26 left nearly 1,500 people dead and more than 5,000 missing. Families searching for their loved ones put up posters bearing names and photographs at hospitals in Kathmandu and travelled to affected areas, including Rasuwa and Nuwakot, in the hope of finding them.

Police deployed trained dogs alongside search-and-rescue personnel to help locate the missing. Among those sent by the Nepal Police Canine Office was Leo, a Labrador retriever that spent 20 days searching for people in the affected areas and assisting rescue teams.

The male dog found two bodies, a human skeleton and several body parts at different locations in Nuwakot.

“Dogs locate bodies by detecting the odour of biological substances released by the human body after death,” said Superintendent of Police Ram Chandra Satyal, chief technical officer at the Canine Office. “Leo performed exceptionally well in the disaster search-and-rescue operation and established himself as an important member of the team.”

For his work, Leo will receive this year’s award for outstanding police dog during Kukur Tihar, the day of the Tihar festival when dogs are honoured. On Sunday, he will be presented with a medal by Deputy Inspector General Om Rana, acting chief of the Nepal Police Crime Investigation Department.

The Nepal Police currently has 107 trained dogs, including Leo. They are trained in four areas: tracking suspects for criminal investigations, detecting firearms and explosives, detecting narcotics, and search and rescue, Satyal said.

Dogs trained to detect drugs and explosives are also deployed at Tribhuvan International Airport, Pokhara International Airport and Gautam Buddha International Airport. Each province has its own canine unit.

“Dogs are also deployed at border crossings to carry out checks,” said central police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle. “They are used during special security operations and for VIP protection as well.”

Some of the dogs in the force have been trained in Nepal, while others have been brought from countries including India, the United States and Thailand.

According to Kafle, police dogs have also proved valuable in criminal investigations. The investigation into the murder of Bhola Sahani in Gadhimai Municipality, Bara, on October 27, 2025, is one example.

Sahani had been missing since the previous day. His body was found the next day beside a pond about 300 metres from his home. As the circumstances appeared suspicious, police brought in a trained dog to assist the investigation.

The dog was given a black hoodie found at the crime scene to sniff. It then led police officers about two kilometres north-west to the house of a resident, Subodh Ram, where it stopped. Investigators later arrested Ram on suspicion of murder, citing other evidence gathered during the investigation.

Police handlers say training methods vary according to a dog’s breed.

“Labradors are well suited to detecting and locating firearms and explosives, so we train them for that work,” said one police dog handler. “German shepherds can work across all four areas. That is why we also call them all-rounder dogs.”

Demand for police dogs in criminal investigations has grown to the point that they are now routinely taken to the scenes of serious crimes.

“Our skin sheds dead cells every minute. Trained dogs can follow the scent left by those cells to track down suspects,” Satyal said.

Police faced criticism for not deploying a sniffer dog during the investigation into the murder of Nirmala Panta, who was found dead in Kanchanpur in July 2018. Residents questioned the police’s handling of the case. Since then, requests for police dogs have increased, particularly in investigations involving serious crimes.

However, a Central Investigation Bureau officer who handles serious criminal cases said dogs could be ineffective in certain conditions. Heavy rain, a crime scene already visited by large numbers of people, or a route that ends at a river can all make it difficult for a dog to pick up a scent.

“The dogs cannot work effectively in every situation. They need to be deployed according to the circumstances,” the officer said. In Panta’s case, the officer added, other people had already entered the crime scene before investigators could consider using a dog.

Canine Office officials say the first 24 hours after a crime are the most effective period for deploying a tracking dog. Beyond that window, investigators cannot expect a consistently successful result.

Yet the expectation that police will deploy dogs at the scene of any serious crime has grown, the CIB officer said. “That also reflects the level of public trust in these dogs,” the officer added.

The Canine Office oversees the dogs’ routine health checks and training. Each morning, they are taken out of their kennels to relieve themselves before being put through exercise and massage sessions. They also take part in daily training exercises for investigative work and practise alongside police officers during parades.

The police have set specific criteria for bringing dogs into service. Operational guidelines give priority to pedigree dogs with a strong sense of smell. They must be between three and 12 months old, as handlers say dogs are easier to train at that age.

Whether donated or purchased, each dog must first be certified healthy by a veterinarian. It then undergoes blood tests and an X-ray examination. Only after receiving the necessary vaccinations and age-appropriate deworming treatment is it admitted to training.

A committee responsible for allocating animal-feed rations oversees the provision of food for the dogs.

The police have also established an Inactive Police Dog Management Committee to decide when dogs should be retired after years of service or when they are no longer fit for deployment. Dogs are retired if they fail a performance assessment conducted by a board tasked with evaluating their working ability.

The Canine Office issues public notices to find people willing to adopt dogs that can no longer serve in the police force. The retired animals are then handed over either for a fee or free of charge.

On November 3, the police handed over Beni, a three-year-four-month-old Labrador retriever, to Police Sub-Inspector Amita Khanal after the dog’s retirement. Khanal paid Rs5,000. An eight-year-two-month-old German shepherd was given to Assistant Sub-Inspector David Dulal free of charge.

Kathmandu, Nov 7: A group of youths and journalists organised a rally in Kathmandu to protest against the alleged press freedom violations. The protests came after police briefly detained three journalists last week and searched newsrooms of several media organisations. Dozens of protesters, wearing black and carrying placards, organised a rally at Maitighar Mandala.

They were carrying placards reading, “Why intervention against media,” “Journalism is not a crime,” and “End suppression against media.” The protesters demanded press freedom, freedom of expression and protection of democratic rights.

Speaking at the rally, youth activist Puskar Bastola accused the Balendra Shah-led government of targeting the media, saying that efforts are being made to snatch people’s freedom of speech.

“As the government is heading towards totalitarianism, we will remain continuously vigilant against such tendencies,” he said Some journalists were briefly detained last week after a few newspapers and online news portals published reports on Prime Minister Balendra Shah seeking the resignation of Nepal Police Inspector General Dan Bahadur Karki for his alleged links to Inam Sapkota, who is in police custody on money laundering and indecent behaviour charges.

Karki was removed earlier this week, and Manoj Kumar KC has been appointed as inspector general. (PTI)

title: Nepal releases details of 2,294 nationals, 171 foreigners missing after Aug 26 floods - BusinessLine
description: Nepal releases details of 2,294 nationals, 171 foreigners missing after Aug 26 floods  BusinessLine
publisher.title: BusinessLine
full_article:
Nepal on Saturday released details of 2,294 nationals from 32 districts, along with 171 foreign nationals from seven countries, who went missing after a devastating flood hit the Himalayan nation on August 26.

The move comes a month after the government ended the 40-day search and rescue operation for victims of the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods, which killed at least 1,455 people and left 5,285 missing, according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).

The authority said the list includes only those whose missing status has been verified by the respective District Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Committees. No further details were available about the remaining missing people who were not named in Saturday's list.

The disaster management authority requested that if any individual listed as missing is found to be alive or has been located, they -- or their immediate family members -- should submit a claim within seven days.

The highest number of missing Nepali nationals, 1,538, are from Rasuwa district, according to the list released by the NDRRMA.

The NDRRMA has also released details of 171 missing foreign nationals from seven countries, excluding India. The authority's website has the complete list.

Among them, 54 are from Malaysia and Ukraine, 33 from Australia, 11 from Russia, nine from South Korea, eight from Germany and two from Italy.

The NDRRMA said it had not yet received a confirmed list of missing Indian nationals from the Indian Embassy.

The list of missing Nepali nationals was prepared based on recommendations from the local governments where they had permanent residence and subsequently approved by the respective District Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Committees.

For missing foreign nationals, the information was obtained through the Department of Consular Services and diplomatic missions based in Nepal or those designated to oversee the country, the authority said.

The NDRRMA will issue a revised notice after receiving details from district administration offices across the 32 districts and relevant diplomatic missions on missing foreign nationals.

Nepal ended the 40-day search-and-rescue operation for victims of the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods on October 5, shifting its focus to rehabilitation and reconstruction in the affected areas.

The flash floods originated near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 and devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal.

The Bhotekoshi River, which flows south from the Himalayan border region, carried the floodwaters downstream, sweeping away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaging hydropower projects.
